text: Welcome to Quantum Programming with Q# and Azure Quantum. If you've worked in Qiskit, you've built circuits by stacking gate calls onto a Python object. Q# asks a different question: what if the quantum program itself, not just the gates you call, were a first-class part of the language? This lesson lays out exactly what that means and when it's the right tool.

Qiskit is a Python SDK — QuantumCircuit and Aer are ordinary Python classes, so a quantum program is really a Python program calling quantum-shaped objects. Q# takes the opposite approach: it's its own compiled language, with its own grammar, its own type checker, and its own compiler, the Quantum Development Kit. A dot-q-s file isn't Python with quantum decorations — it's a different file type entirely. And in Q#, an operation is a language construct with a declared signature that the compiler enforces, the same way it enforces how any function composes with another.

Because Q# is statically typed, a mismatched return type or an operation called with the wrong number of qubits gets caught at compile time, before anything touches a simulator or real hardware. The Controlled and Adjoint functors show what this buys you concretely: write an operation, and Q# can automatically derive its controlled version or its inverse without you writing a second implementation. Qiskit has no equivalent — you'd build that controlled or inverse circuit yourself, gate by gate.

The other genuinely new piece is the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator. Before fault-tolerant hardware exists at useful scale, the real question is usually how many logical qubits, how many physical qubits after error correction, and how much wall-clock time an algorithm would need under a stated hardware profile. The resource estimator answers exactly that, without executing on any real or simulated hardware at all. It's a first-class, well-supported workflow in the Q# and Azure Quantum stack — nothing comparable ships as a core feature of Qiskit.

So when do you reach for which? If you're writing a quantum kernel that plugs into an existing Python data or machine learning pipeline, Qiskit's Python-native ecosystem is the pragmatic choice — there's no serialization boundary to cross. If you need a credible qubit-count and runtime estimate for a hardware proposal, or you want the compiler itself enforcing correctness on a nontrivial program, Q# and Azure Quantum are built for exactly that. And they're not mutually exclusive — later in this course you'll use the qsharp Python package to call Q# operations from inside a Python workflow.
Next lesson, we get your machine actually set up: the two real ways to write and run Q# today, and installing the modern Quantum Development Kit.
